html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. AI: artificial intelligence

  • The main fact-checking techniques: primary sources, grounding, cross-checking, recalculation, sampling
  • How to use web search and citations safely
  • How much checking an output needs, based on stakes
  • When a human must review before anything is sent, published or decided

2Fact-Checking Techniques

Running case

Cedarbrook's Press Release

  • Communications asks Claude to draft a release on the company's carbon-reduction results
  • The draft contains three statistics and a quote attributed to an industry body
  • Before publishing, the team traces each number to the sustainability report and each quote to the original
Technique How it works Best for
Check the primary source Open the official document, regulation, dataset or website and compare Citations, legal and policy statements, quotes
Ground Claude in your documents Upload or paste the source and tell Claude to answer only from it and to quote the supporting lines Summaries and Q&A on known material
Ask for sources, then check them Request links or titles; open them yourself; a source Claude cannot supply is a red flag Research claims
Cross-check with independent sources Confirm key facts in two or more trustworthy places Statistics, market facts, dates
Recalculate Redo totals and percentages from the raw data in a spreadsheet Numbers and tables
Spot-check a sample Check a random subset of items against the source; widen if errors appear Long lists, bulk summaries
Test the artifact Run the formula, script or macro on sample data with a known answer Technical outputs
Second pair of eyes A colleague or subject-matter expert reviews High-stakes content

  • Asking Claude "are you sure?" is not verification: it may repeat the error or change a correct answer.
  • Asking Claude to find problems in its own draft is a useful first pass, but not a substitute for your check against a source.
  • Quote-first prompting: "First extract the exact lines that answer the question, then answer." This makes unsupported claims easier to spot.
  • Allow "I don't know": tell Claude it may answer "the document does not say" instead of guessing.
Exam tip

The strongest checks go outside Claude: an authoritative source, a recalculation, a test run or a qualified person.

3Using Web Search and Citations

  • With web search on, Claude grounds answers in live web content and gives citations and source links. A visible indicator shows when it is searching.
  • Review the cited sources. The Help Center warns that original sites may hold context or detail not in Claude's synthesis, and that answer quality depends on the sources it used.
  • Ask for multiple sources and verify important information against authoritative ones.
  • Prefer primary and official sources (regulators, standards bodies, the company itself) over blogs.
  • Dates matter: check how recent a source is.
  • Include "search the web" in the prompt to make sure it searches, or tell it not to when you want it to use only your documents.
  • Research mode produces a longer report with citations; the same rule applies: open the sources for the claims you will rely on.

Exam tip

A cited answer is easier to verify, not already verified. The step that counts is that a person reads the source.

4How Much Checking Is Enough?

Match the depth of review to the risk.

Factor Lower risk Higher risk
Stakes Internal brainstorm Legal, medical, financial, safety, people decisions
Audience You alone Customers, regulators, the public, the board
Reversibility Easy to fix Sent, published, filed, paid
Source reliability You provided and trust the source Claude answered from memory
Novelty Routine, repeated task with a proven prompt New topic or unfamiliar domain

  • Low stakes and reversible (a brainstorm list): a quick read.
  • Medium (an internal report): spot-check the key figures.
  • High and hard to undo (a regulatory filing, a customer-facing claim, a contract summary): check every claim and add expert review.

5When Human Review Is Required

A qualified human must review before use when:

  1. The output supports legal, medical, financial, safety or compliance decisions
  2. It affects people: hiring, promotion, credit, benefits, grades, access to services
  3. It will be published or sent externally under the company's name
  4. It involves regulated or sensitive data (Module 13)
  5. The action is irreversible or costly (payments, deletions, sending to many customers)
  6. Claude's answer is uncertain, contradictory or outside the checker's expertise
  7. Organizational policy says so
  • Anthropic's Usage Policy lists high-risk uses (legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education, public benefits). For these a qualified human-in-the-loop must meaningfully review the recommendation before it is delivered or acted on and must be able to change it, and the affected person must be told AI was involved.
  • The human must be qualified: a lawyer reviews legal text, an accountant reviews financial figures. Skimming is not review.
  • Document how AI was used and who reviewed the result.
  • Keep the person accountable: Claude drafts; the human owns the decision.
Exam tip

In scenarios about regulated advice, people decisions or external publication, the right answer includes review by a qualified person before use, never "send it, Claude is usually right".

6Exam Q&A

S1A press release draft contains a statistic and a quote attributed to a trade body. What is the best validation?

  • AReword the quote so that it sounds more natural and fits the tone of the release
  • BPublish the release now and correct the figures later if anyone complains about them
  • CTrace the statistic and the quote to the original sources before publishing
  • DAsk Claude whether it is sure
Show the answer

Answer: C. Verify claims against the original sources, especially for external publication.

S2Which prompt best reduces unsupported claims when summarizing an uploaded policy?

  • A"Summarize this policy."
  • B"Answer only from the policy, quote the lines you used, and say if it does not cover a point."
  • C"Summarize this and be confident."
  • D"Summarize this using everything you know about the topic, not only what the policy says, please."
Show the answer

Answer: B. Grounding in the document, quoting and allowing "not covered" make errors visible.

S3An associate asks Claude "are you sure?" and Claude says yes. What does that prove?

  • ANothing reliable; the claim still needs to be checked against a source
  • BThe answer is complete
  • CThe answer is verified
  • DThe answer is unbiased
Show the answer

Answer: A. Self-reported certainty is not a validation method, so the claim still has to be checked against an independent source.

S4Claude's web-search answer includes citations. What is the best next step for a claim you will rely on?

  • ADelete the citations to save space
  • BOpen the cited source and confirm the claim and its date
  • CAssume the citations make it correct
  • DAsk Claude to search again
Show the answer

Answer: B. Citations make verification possible; a person must follow them.

S5Which output needs the deepest review?

  • AA list of ten possible team-lunch themes for the next monthly meeting
  • BA brainstorm of hashtag ideas
  • CA draft agenda for an internal stand-up meeting that will not leave the team
  • DA summary of a customer contract to be sent to the client
Show the answer

Answer: D. External, contract-related content carries high stakes and is hard to undo.

S6Which TWO situations require review by a qualified human before use? Select TWO.

  • ADrafting a casual internal thank-you note
  • BScreening job applicants where the output would drive rejection decisions
  • CBrainstorming event names
  • DSummarizing medical guidance that staff will use with patients
  • EReformatting a to-do list
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Medical guidance and employment decisions are high-risk uses that need a qualified human reviewer.

S7Claude produces a spreadsheet formula for commission calculations. What is the best validation?

  • AApply it to the full payroll file immediately
  • BAsk Claude to explain the formula in more detail and skip testing
  • CTrust it, as formulas are always right
  • DTest it on sample rows where the correct result is known
Show the answer

Answer: D. Test technical outputs on known cases before real use.

S8Why should a human reviewer of a legal summary be qualified?

  • ABecause company rules say that any employee in the department may review legal text
  • BTo make the review take longer so that the work looks careful and thorough to managers
  • CBecause Claude cannot summarize law
  • DBecause meaningful review needs the expertise to spot errors that look plausible
Show the answer

Answer: D. Review is only meaningful when the reviewer can recognize substantive errors.

S9A team uses Claude to draft decision letters about benefits. What does the Usage Policy expect?

  • AA qualified human reviews before delivery, and the affected people are told AI was involved
  • BReview only when the letter is rejected
  • CDisclosure only if requested
  • DNo human involvement and no disclosure
Show the answer

Answer: A. High-risk uses need human-in-the-loop review and disclosure that AI was involved.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Strongest checks Primary source · recalculation · test run · qualified reviewer
Weak checks "Are you sure?" · polish · self-rated confidence
Grounding Answer only from the provided source; quote lines; allow "not covered"
Web search Citations help; open the sources; prefer primary and recent
Depth Scale with stakes, audience, reversibility, source reliability, novelty
Human review needed Legal, medical, financial, safety, people decisions, external publication, regulated data, irreversible actions, policy
High-risk uses Qualified human reviews and can change it; tell affected people AI was involved
Accountability Claude drafts; a named person decides
